stages.title: Latitude and longitude
stages.hook: Every place on Earth has an address made only of two numbers. How could numbers pin down a spot on a round planet?
explain: Geographers draw imaginary lines on the globe. Lines that run east-west are lines of latitude. The equator is 0° latitude, the poles are 90° north and 90° south.
Lines of longitude run from pole to pole. The prime meridian, at 0° longitude, passes through Greenwich in London. Longitude is measured up to 180° east and 180° west.
A place is given as latitude first, then longitude. Nairobi is near 1° S, 37° E. That means just south of the equator and east of the prime meridian.
One degree of latitude is always about 111 km on the ground. Degrees of longitude get shorter toward the poles, because the lines meet there.

example.q: Roughly how far is it from the equator (0°) to the North Pole (90° N)?
steps: The change in latitude is 90 degrees.
Each degree of latitude is about 111 km.
Multiply: 90 × 111 = 9,990 km.

analogies.home: Think of rows and columns of seats in a cinema. Row and seat number find your place. Latitude and longitude do the same for Earth.
analogies.sea: A ship's captain reports position as latitude and longitude, so rescuers know where to go.
analogies.tech: A phone shows coordinates in the same way, using satellites to work them out.
analogies.city: A city street grid with avenue and street numbers works like a small version of this idea.

stages.mnemonic: Latitude is like a ladder (rungs go across), longitude runs long from top to bottom.
terms: Distance north or south of the equator, in degrees.
Distance east or west of the prime meridian, in degrees.
The 0° latitude line around the middle of Earth.
A pair of numbers that give an exact place.

misc.wrong: Longitude lines are parallel like latitude lines.
misc.right: Latitude lines are parallel. Longitude lines are not parallel; they all meet at the two poles.

stages.limits: There are two ways to write degrees: decimals or degrees and minutes. They describe the same places.

questions.q: Why do we need both latitude and longitude to name a place exactly?

questions.why: One number gives a whole line of places. Two lines cross at one point.

panel.q: A friend says two cities with the same latitude must be close together. Is she right? Explain.

teach.topic: How latitude and longitude give an exact place
teach.model: Latitude lines run east-west and measure distance from the equator. Longitude lines run from pole to pole and measure distance from the prime meridian. A place is where one of each cross, so two numbers find it.

stages.title: Map scales and symbols
stages.hook: A map of a whole country fits on one page. How can it still be used to measure real distances?
explain: A map is a small picture of a big place. The scale tells how much smaller. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground, which is 0.5 km.
A bar scale is a little ruler on the map. A large-scale map shows a small area with lots of detail, like a town. A small-scale map shows a large area with little detail, like a continent.
Map symbols are small pictures or colours that stand for things. The key lists them. Blue usually means water. Green may mean forest or parks. Contour lines show height.
Contour lines join places of the same height. Lines close together mean steep ground. Lines far apart mean gentle ground.

example.q: A map has scale 1:100,000. Two towns are 6 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
steps: 1 cm on the map is 100,000 cm on the ground.
So 1 cm = 1 km.
6 cm = 6 km.

analogies.home: A plan of your room on paper uses a scale: 1 cm for each metre, for instance.
analogies.city: A city bus map is small-scale and simple. A street map of one district shows each building.
analogies.sport: A football pitch diagram on a coach's board uses a scale.
analogies.tech: On a phone map, zooming in changes the scale. The same place gets more detail.

stages.mnemonic: Large scale, large detail, small area. Small scale, small detail, big area.
terms: The link between a distance on the map and the real distance.
A list that explains the map symbols.
A line joining places of equal height.
A small picture or colour that stands for something real.

misc.wrong: A large-scale map shows a large area.
misc.right: A large-scale map shows a small area in great detail. A small-scale map shows a large area.

stages.limits: No flat map can show real distances perfectly everywhere. Scales are best for small areas.

panel.model: Measure the straight line between the towns with a ruler or string. Lay it along the bar scale or multiply by the scale to turn it into real kilometres.

teach.topic: How map scale and symbols work
teach.model: A scale shows how much a map is shrunk. 1 cm on the map can stand for a certain distance on the ground. Symbols and a key show what things are. Contour lines show height.

stages.title: World regions and countries
stages.hook: Is Russia in Europe or Asia? Is it fair that one country can be in two continents?
explain: Geographers sort the world into regions: groups of countries that share location, climate or history. Examples are West Africa, Western Europe, South Asia, Central America and Oceania.
There are around 195 countries today: about 193 member states of the United Nations and a few others. Numbers change a little as politics change. Africa has the most UN member states, 54.
Some countries sit in two continents. Russia lies in Europe and Asia. Turkey is in both too. Egypt is mostly in Africa, with the Sinai part in Asia.
Region names help us compare places. For example, the Middle East is a region, not a continent, and people define it a little differently.

example.q: Egypt has land in Africa and Asia. Is it correct to say it is in two continents?
steps: Most of Egypt is in northeast Africa.
The Sinai Peninsula is east of the Suez Canal, in Asia.
So Egypt is a transcontinental country.
example.a: Yes, mostly Africa with a small part in Asia

analogies.home: Rooms on one floor of a house form a group. Countries in a region are neighbours like that.
analogies.city: A city has districts: north, central, harbour. Regions are like districts of the world.
analogies.sport: Football has continental competitions, such as those in Africa, Asia and South America.
analogies.nature: Regions with the same climate often share similar plants and animals.

stages.mnemonic: A region is a neighbourhood of countries.
terms: A group of places that share something, like location or climate.
A land with its own government and borders.

misc.wrong: Everyone agrees where each region begins and ends.
misc.right: Region borders are drawn differently by different people and organisations.

stages.limits: The number of countries depends on who counts and whether disputed areas are included.

stages.title: Earth's internal structure
stages.hook: We have never dug to the centre of Earth. How do we know what is inside?
explain: Earth is built in layers like an onion. The thin outer layer is the crust, the rock we live on. Under it is the thick mantle, mostly hot solid rock that can flow very slowly.
In the middle is the core. The outer core is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel. The inner core is solid metal, because the pressure is enormous.
From the surface to the centre is about 6,371 km. The crust is thin: roughly 5 to 10 km under the oceans and up to about 70 km under big mountains.
Scientists learn about the layers from earthquake waves. Waves bend and speed up or slow down as they pass through different materials. We also study volcanoes and rocks.

example.q: Earth's radius is about 6,371 km. The crust under land averages about 35 km thick. About what fraction of the radius is it?
steps: Divide the thickness by the radius: 35 ÷ 6,371.
That is about 0.0055.
Less than 1 percent.
example.a: About half of one percent, very thin

analogies.home: An egg has a shell, white and yolk. Earth has crust, mantle and core.
analogies.farm: A peach has skin, flesh and a stone, like crust, mantle and core.
analogies.tech: Doctors use scans to see inside a body without cutting. Earthquake waves work like a scan of Earth.
analogies.nature: A tree has bark and layers inside, seen in its rings.

stages.mnemonic: Crust is the crumb, mantle is the middle, core is the centre.
terms: The thin, solid outer layer of Earth.
The thick layer of hot rock under the crust.
A layer of liquid metal around the centre.
The solid metal ball at the centre.

misc.wrong: The mantle is a sea of liquid lava.
misc.right: The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly. Only small parts melt to form magma.

stages.limits: Our knowledge comes from indirect evidence. The deepest drill hole is only about 12 km, far short of the mantle.

stages.title: Rocks and landforms
stages.hook: A pebble on a beach may once have been part of a mountain. How can rock change?
explain: Rocks are of three main kinds. Igneous rocks form when hot melted rock cools and hardens. Granite and basalt are examples.
Sedimentary rocks form when bits of sand, mud and shells settle in layers and are pressed together over a long time. Sandstone, limestone and shale are examples. Fossils are found in them.
Metamorphic rocks form when heat and pressure change old rocks without melting them completely. Marble comes from limestone. Slate comes from shale.
Over millions of years, rocks can change from one type to another. This is called the rock cycle. Wind, water and ice break rocks down in a process called weathering.

example.q: A layer of sand is buried and pressed for millions of years into rock. What type is it?
steps: The rock is made of sand pressed together.
That is how sedimentary rocks form.
Sandstone is an example.

analogies.home: Cooling chocolate that was melted becomes hard again, like igneous rock.
analogies.farm: Soil layers settle one on top of another, like sedimentary layers.
analogies.nature: Waves slowly turn big stones into small pebbles and sand.
analogies.city: Marble floors and slate roofs are metamorphic rocks used in building.

misc.right: Rocks slowly change over millions of years in the rock cycle.

stages.limits: The rock cycle has many paths. A rock does not follow a fixed order.

stages.title: Water cycle and drainage systems
stages.hook: The water you drink today may once have been in a dinosaur-age sea. How does water keep moving?
explain: Water is always moving in the water cycle. The Sun heats oceans, lakes and rivers and water evaporates into the air as invisible vapour. Plants also give out water vapour, called transpiration.
High in the sky, the air cools. Vapour condenses into tiny drops that form clouds. When drops get big and heavy, they fall as precipitation: rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Some water runs over the ground into streams. Some soaks into the ground. All water eventually flows back to the sea or evaporates again.
A drainage basin is all the land that drains into one river. The high ground between two basins is a watershed or divide. A river and its tributaries, the smaller rivers that join it, form a network.

example.q: Rain falls on a mountain and flows into river A. Rain on the other side flows to river B. What is the ridge between called?
steps: Water runs downhill on both sides.
The high line separates two drainage basins.
That line is the watershed.

analogies.home: Steam from a kettle meets a cold window and turns back into drops. That is condensation.
analogies.farm: Farmers watch for rain and use irrigation, taking water from rivers.
analogies.city: Storm drains in a city carry rain to rivers, a small drainage system.
analogies.nature: A leaf gives out water vapour that joins the clouds.

stages.mnemonic: Evaporate up, condense in clouds, precipitate down, collect, repeat.

misc.wrong: Clouds are made of water vapour.
misc.right: Water vapour is invisible. Clouds are made of tiny liquid drops or ice crystals.

stages.limits: The cycle has no starting point. Total water on Earth stays nearly the same, but where it is changes.

stages.title: Climate and vegetation zones
stages.hook: Why are there rainforests near the equator but ice near the poles?
explain: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years (30 years is common). Weather is just what is happening today. Climate depends on latitude, height, distance from the sea and winds.
Near the equator the Sun is high in the sky all year, so it is hot. Toward the poles the Sun is low, so sunlight is spread out and it is cold. Mountains are colder than lowlands at the same latitude.

Natural vegetation follows climate. Tropical rainforests are hot and wet all year. Savannas are warm with a dry season and have grass and scattered trees. Deserts get very little rain. Temperate regions have four seasons with forests or grassland. Tundra is cold, treeless and frozen for long periods.
The Köppen system is a famous way of grouping climates. It uses temperature and rainfall.

example.q: A place is hot all year and rains almost every day. Which vegetation do you expect?
steps: Hot all year means tropical.
Rain all year gives lots of water.
That grows dense rainforest.

analogies.home: A room near the heater is warm, a room by an open window is cool. Latitude is like distance from the heater.
analogies.farm: Farmers choose crops to fit the climate: rice in wet warm places, wheat in drier temperate ones.
analogies.city: People in hot climates build houses with thick walls and shade; people in cold ones insulate.
analogies.nature: Cacti store water in deserts; spruce trees shed snow in cold forests.

stages.mnemonic: Hot and wet: forest. Hot and dry: desert. Cold: tundra.
terms: Average weather of a place over many years.
The plants that grow naturally in a place.
A place with very little rainfall.

misc.right: A desert is defined by low rainfall. Antarctica and parts of the Gobi are cold deserts.

stages.limits: Climate zones have blurry edges and are shifting as the climate changes.

stages.title: Population and settlements
stages.hook: More than eight billion people share Earth, but they are not spread evenly. Why do some places teem with people and others are almost empty?
explain: The world population is about eight billion people. Population density is the number of people per square kilometre. It is found by dividing population by area.

People mostly live where it is easy to grow food and find water: river valleys, coasts and fertile plains. South and East Asia, Europe and the Nile valley are densely settled. Deserts, polar lands, high mountains and thick rainforests have few people.

Settlements are places where people live. A rural settlement is in the countryside: a farm, hamlet or village. An urban settlement is a town or city. Today more than half of all people live in cities.
Settlements start where there is a reason: water, flat land, a river crossing, a port, a mine or a safe hill.

example.q: A country has 6,000,000 people living on 20,000 km². What is its population density?
steps: Density = population ÷ area.

analogies.home: A crowded room has high density. A big hall with a few people has low density.
analogies.city: Apartment towers fit many people on small land.
analogies.farm: Farm villages sit near fields and wells, so work and water are close.

misc.right: Density depends on people and area. Canada is huge but has a low density; Bangladesh is small and has a high one.

stages.limits: Averages hide differences. Most of Egypt's people live along the Nile, even though the average density looks low.

stages.title: Natural resources
stages.hook: A phone, a bicycle and a loaf of bread all start in nature. Where do their ingredients come from?
explain: Natural resources are materials from nature that people use, such as water, soil, forests, fish, minerals and fuels. We also use energy from the Sun, wind and moving water.

Renewable resources can be replaced naturally in a human lifetime if we use them carefully: wood from managed forests, fish, solar power and wind. Non-renewable resources, such as coal, oil, natural gas and metal ores, take millions of years to form, so once used they are gone for practical purposes.

Resources are not spread evenly. Oil is concentrated in places like the Arabian Peninsula; copper is found in Chile, Peru and Zambia; fertile soil is found on big plains. Some countries sell resources to others.
Using resources wisely means reducing waste, reusing, recycling and choosing renewables. This is called sustainability.

example.q: A village uses a forest for firewood. Each year the trees that grow back equal the wood cut. Is the resource being used sustainably?
steps: Wood is renewable.
Cut wood equals regrown wood.
The forest is not shrinking, so it is sustainable.

analogies.home: Saving water by turning off the tap means the water lasts.
analogies.farm: Farmers rotate crops to keep soil healthy for future seasons.
analogies.city: Recycling bins collect metal, glass and paper to make new things.
analogies.tech: Phones contain metals like copper and gold that can be recycled.

stages.mnemonic: Renewable can regrow, non-renewable will go.
terms: A material from nature that people use.
Replaced naturally in a short time.

misc.wrong: Renewable resources can never run out.
misc.right: Renewables can be used up if we take them faster than they are replaced, as with overfishing.

stages.limits: Whether a resource is renewable depends on how fast we use it compared to how fast it recovers.
